Executive Summary and Macroeconomic Architecture of Canadian R&D Incentives

Canada maintains one of the most mature, generous, and technically rigorous research and development (R&D) fiscal incentive architectures in the industrialized world. The cornerstone of this framework is the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, which supports more than 22,000 claiming businesses nationally—including approximately 4,000 claimants in Quebec alone—and distributes upwards of $4 billion annually in tax assistance. Co-administered by the Department of Finance Canada, which establishes statutory tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which executes technical and financial compliance reviews, the SR&ED program operates as a dual-mechanism entitlement under the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945. Rather than functioning as a discretionary competitive grant, SR&ED is a statutory right: any taxpayer performing qualifying scientific or technological investigation within Canada that satisfies the legislative criteria of subsection 248(1) of the ITA and adheres to the prescribed filing deadlines is legally entitled to both an immediate income tax deduction under section 37 and an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under section 127.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential structural modernization since the Jobs and Growth Act, 2012 (Bill C-45). For more than a decade following the 2012–2014 reforms—which had eliminated capital expenditures from the SR&ED base, reduced the general corporate ITC rate from 20% to 15%, imposed an 80% inclusion limit on arm's-length contractor payments, and lowered the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) overhead rate from 65% to 55%—economists and industry stakeholders raised concerns that Canada's innovation policy disproportionately favoured early-stage micro-enterprises while penalizing domestic scale-ups that went public or invested in capital-intensive R&D. Specifically, because the enhanced 35% refundable ITC was strictly restricted to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and phased out entirely once prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reached $50 million, high-growth Canadian technology and life-sciences firms faced a severe fiscal cliff upon executing an Initial Public Offering (IPO) on a Canadian exchange or scaling their balance sheets.

To address this structural disincentive and stem the migration of Canadian intellectual property (IP) to foreign jurisdictions, the Department of Finance Canada initiated a two-phase public consultation process in 2024. Phase 1 ran from January 31, 2024, to April 15, 2024, seeking stakeholder input on modernizing the SR&ED architecture, ensuring IP retention within Canada, and recalibrating eligibility criteria. On April 16, 2024, the federal government tabled Budget 2024: Fairness for Every Generation, committing $600 million over four years beginning in 2025—with $150 million per year on an ongoing basis—to enhance the SR&ED program and launching Phase 2 consultations through May 27, 2024.

The specific legislative architecture of these reforms crystallized across the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (tabled on December 16, 2024), subsequent draft legislative amendments released in August 2025, the 2025 Federal Budget, and the enacting statute, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the modernized federal SR&ED regime introduces four transformative structural shifts that reshape the innovation ecosystem. First, the annual expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC—which stood at $3 million for decades—was initially proposed in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement to increase to $4.5 million alongside an expansion of the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the legacy $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million. Budget 2025 measures (tabled on November 4, 2025) enacted under Bill C-15 further elevated the enhanced 35% expenditure limit to $6 million per year for taxation years starting on or after December 16, 2024. Second, eliminating the historic "IPO penalty," the enhanced 35% refundable ITC is no longer restricted exclusively to CCPCs. It now extends to eligible Canadian public corporations—defined as corporations resident in Canada throughout the year whose shares are listed on a designated stock exchange (or that have elected to be public corporations) and that are not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons.

Third, reversing the post-2013 capital exclusion, depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (and lease costs first becoming payable on or after that date) is once again eligible for both the section 37 income deduction and the section 127 ITC, provided the property is intended either to be used all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life in performing SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all of its value in performing SR&ED in Canada. For CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations claiming the 35% rate, ITCs earned on restored capital expenditures are eligible for partial refundability at a rate of 40%. Fourth, recognising that modern software and artificial intelligence (AI) R&D relies heavily on high-density compute rather than physical laboratory consumables, these SR&ED reforms complement Budget 2024's $2.4 billion AI package—featuring the $2 billion AI Compute Access Fund and Canadian AI Sovereign Compute Strategy, $200 million for sectoral AI adoption, and $100 million for the National Research Council's AI Assist Program—as well as temporary 100% accelerated Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) write-offs for patents, data network infrastructure equipment, and general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment acquired between April 16, 2024, and January 1, 2027.

From a second- and third-order analytical perspective, the convergence of these reforms fundamentally alters corporate finance and R&D location decisions in Canada. Under the pre-2024 regime, a Canadian technology company contemplating a public listing on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) faced an immediate loss of up to $1.05 million in annual cash refunds (35% of $3 million), shifting overnight to a 15% non-refundable credit that provided zero liquidity until the company generated Part I taxable income. By extending the 35% refundable tier to Canadian-resident, domestically controlled public corporations and expanding the taxable capital phase-out ceiling to $75 million, the Department of Finance has removed the tax-induced bias toward remaining private or selling early to foreign acquirers. Simultaneously, restoring capital expenditures to the SR&ED base—coupled with provincial harmonization in jurisdictions such as Ontario, which updated the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) to include 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024—re-establishes fiscal parity between software firms (whose costs are predominantly current salaries) and hardware, clean-technology, bio-manufacturing, and advanced manufacturing enterprises that must acquire specialized testing rigs and pilot-scale machinery.
Federal Statutory Framework and the Definition of SR&ED
The Dual-Pillar Statutory Mechanism: Section 37 and Section 127 of the Income Tax Act

The federal SR&ED incentive operates through two distinct but interconnected statutory provisions of the Income Tax Act (Canada), supplemented by Part XXIX (Section 2900 and Section 2902) of the Income Tax Regulations. The first pillar is Section 37 (Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures). Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA—specifically paragraph 37(1)(a) for current expenditures—a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool all qualifying SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada (along with limited permissible salary expenditures incurred outside Canada under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)) into a dedicated tax pool. Unlike ordinary capital expenses that must be amortized over multi-year Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) schedules, expenditures in the section 37 pool may be deducted in full in the current taxation year to reduce income from a business for tax purposes, or carried forward indefinitely to shelter taxable income in any future taxation year. This indefinite carryforward protects early-stage, pre-revenue R&D enterprises from losing the tax value of their deductions due to the standard 20-year expiry period applicable to ordinary non-capital losses.

The second pillar is Section 127 (Investment Tax Credit). Once the allowable SR&ED expenditure pool is established under section 37, those expenditures—adjusted for specific statutory inclusions (such as the Prescribed Proxy Amount for overhead under the proxy method) and statutory exclusions or reductions (such as the 20% reduction on arm's-length contractor payments, unpaid amounts remaining outstanding after 180 days, and government or non-government assistance)—form the taxpayer's qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Under subsections 127(5) and 127(10.1), the taxpayer earns an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit equal to 15% or 35% of these qualified expenditures. Non-refundable ITCs are first applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable in the current year; any unused non-refundable ITC balance may be carried back three (3) taxation years or carried forward twenty (20) taxation years to offset Part I tax. Crucially, any federal SR&ED ITC claimed—whether applied against Part I tax or received as a cash refund—reduces the pool in the subsequent taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e), in the same way that government assistance as defined in subsection 127(9) reduces it under paragraph 37(1)(d), reducing the section 37 deduction pool (or being included in taxable business income under paragraph 12(1)(t) to the extent the section 37 pool is reduced below zero) in the following taxation year.

body.text: Statutory Anatomy of Subsection 248(1): The Three Pillars, Support Work, and Exclusions

To qualify for SR&ED tax incentives, claimed activities must satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set forth in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. The statute mandates an overarching threshold requirement: the work must constitute a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Furthermore, that systematic investigation must fall within one of three primary legal pillars. The first pillar, basic research under paragraph 248(1)(a), encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, such as theoretical or empirical investigations into fundamental natural phenomena in physics, chemistry, or molecular biology. The second pillar, applied research under paragraph 248(1)(b), covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, bridging fundamental science and industrial utility—such as investigating the electrochemical degradation mechanisms of a novel solid-state battery electrolyte with the specific aim of extending electric vehicle battery lifecycles.

The third and commercially dominant pillar is experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c), defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Over 95% of industrial SR&ED claims in Canada are filed under paragraph 248(1)(c). Crucially, the statutory phrase "including incremental improvements thereto" confirms that a taxpayer does not need to invent a disruptive, world-first commercial product; rather, resolving an underlying technological uncertainty to achieve an incremental advancement in the technological capability of an existing manufacturing process, software architecture, or chemical formulation fully satisfies the statute.
Commensurate Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d))

Once a core project is established under paragraph (a), (b), or (c), paragraph 248(1)(d) expands the scope of eligible SR&ED to include eight specific categories of support work: (i) engineering, (ii) design, (iii) operations research, (iv) mathematical analysis, (v) computer programming, (vi) data collection, (vii) testing, or (viii) psychological research. However, such work qualifies only to the extent that it is "commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of" the basic research, applied research, or experimental development that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. In CRA audit practice, this "commensurate and directly in support" requirement prevents taxpayers from claiming general commercial software coding, user-interface development, or CAD mechanical drafting that extends beyond what is strictly necessary to construct an experimental prototype and test the scientific or technological hypothesis.
Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k))

Even where a project involves genuine experimental development, subsection 248(1) explicitly carves out seven categories of commercial and routine activities that are statutorily barred from qualifying as SR&ED. Specifically, eligible SR&ED does not include work with respect to market research or sales promotion under paragraph 248(1)(e) (such as customer surveys, UI/UX aesthetic testing, or business analytics); quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes under paragraph 248(1)(f) (such as standard QA/QC compliance testing against established ISO or CSA standards where no technological uncertainty is being investigated); or research in the social sciences or the humanities under paragraph 248(1)(g) (including economics, business management, law, and behavioural marketing).

Similarly, the statute excludes prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas under paragraph 248(1)(h), as geological exploration is governed separately by Canadian Exploration Expense (CEE) and Canadian Development Expense (CDE) regimes, although developing novel extraction technologies or metallurgical processes can still qualify as experimental development. Finally, subsection 248(1) excludes the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process under paragraph 248(1)(i) (though experimental production trials conducted on a commercial line strictly to test a technological hypothesis remain eligible for the incremental experimental portion); style changes under paragraph 248(1)(j) (cosmetic or aesthetic modifications lacking underlying technological uncertainty); and routine data collection under paragraph 248(1)(k) (gathering logs, telemetry, or environmental measurements without a systematic experimental hypothesis).
Federal Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Expenditure Caps, and 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms
Comparative Analysis of Claimant Categories and Credit Tiers

The rate and refundability of the federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit under section 127 of the ITA depend on the legal classification of the claimant, its ownership structure, its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, and the nature of the expenditure (current versus capital). Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 (implementing the reforms effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024), the federal regime distinguishes between four primary claimant tiers.

The first tier comprises Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), defined under subsection 125(7) of the ITA as private corporations that are Canadian corporations other than corporations controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than prescribed venture capital corporations), or by any combination thereof. Qualifying CCPCs earn the enhanced 35% federal ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit. For current expenditures within the expenditure limit, the 35% ITC is 100% refundable. For restored capital expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024, within the expenditure limit, the 35% ITC is 40% refundable. On qualified expenditures exceeding the annual expenditure limit, CCPCs earn the basic 15% ITC, which is 40% refundable for "qualifying corporations" (CCPCs whose prior-year taxable income does not exceed their qualifying income limit) and non-refundable for CCPCs exceeding that limit.

The second tier—newly created for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024—consists of Eligible Canadian Public Corporations. Introduced via the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and enacted under Bill C-15, an "eligible Canadian public corporation" is defined as a corporation that, throughout the taxation year, is resident in Canada, has a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or has elected to be a public corporation), and is not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons. These corporations now qualify for the enhanced 35% ITC up to the annual Expenditure Limit on the exact same terms as CCPCs, including 100% refundability on current expenditures and 40% refundability on restored capital expenditures within the limit, subject to a phase-out of the limit based on average annual gross revenue for the three preceding taxation years between $15 million and $75 million under subsection 127(10.6).

The third tier encompasses Other Corporations, including foreign-controlled subsidiaries, public corporations controlled by non-residents, and large domestic corporations whose prior-year taxable capital exceeds the $75 million upper phase-out threshold. These corporations earn a flat 15% non-refundable federal ITC on all qualified SR&ED expenditures (both current and restored capital). While non-refundable in cash, this 15% credit directly offsets federal Part I corporate income tax payable and can be carried back 3 years or forward 20 years.

The fourth tier covers Individuals (Sole Proprietorships), Unincorporated Businesses, and Certain Trusts. Unincorporated taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada earn a 15% federal ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures. After offsetting federal Part I tax payable for the year, 40% of the remaining unused 15% ITC is refundable in cash (yielding an effective cash refund rate of 6% for non-taxable individuals), while the remaining 60% may be carried back 3 years or forward 20 years. Partnerships cannot claim the ITC directly because a partnership is not a separate taxable person under the ITA; instead, section 37 deductions and section 127 ITCs are allocated to the active corporate or individual partners at year-end.

body.text: Mathematical Formulation of the Expenditure Limit Phase-Out

Under subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA, the annual Expenditure Limit available to a qualifying CCPC (and its associated corporations) is subject to a gradual straight-line reduction when the corporation's (and associated group's) taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds the lower phase-out threshold; for eligible Canadian public corporations, subsection 127(10.6) applies the same formula to average annual gross revenue for the three preceding taxation years.

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024 (under the legacy $3 million limit and $10 million to $50 million taxable capital phase-out band), the Expenditure Limit (EL) was computed as: EL = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $10,000,000.
Under this legacy formula, every $100,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $10 million reduced the $3 million expenditure limit by $7,500, extinguishing the limit completely at $50 million.

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the taxable capital phase-out range expanded to begin at $15,000,000 and terminate at $75,000,000 (a $60,000,000 phase-out span). Applying the initial 2024 Fall Economic Statement limit ($4,500,000), the formula is: EL = $4,500,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000.

Under the expanded $6,000,000 expenditure limit enacted for post-December 16, 2024 taxation years under the 2025 Budget and Bill C-15 framework ($6,000,000), the generalized statutory formula with maximum limit and prorated for short taxation years of fewer than 51 weeks by the number of days in the year (D) is expressed as: EL = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000 × D ÷ 365, where A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000.

This expansion has profound balance-sheet implications for capital-intensive Canadian scale-ups. Because "taxable capital employed in Canada" includes capital stock (preferred and common equity), retained earnings, contributed surplus, and long-term debt, venture-backed biotechnology or clean-tech startups that raised a $45 million Series B or Series C equity financing round previously saw their $3 million SR&ED expenditure limit reduced by 87.5% (down to $375,000) in the year following the financing. Under the modernized $15 million–$75 million phase-out band, a company with $45 million in prior-year taxable capital retains exactly 50% of its expanded expenditure limit ($2.25 million under the $4.5 million cap, or $3.0 million under the $6.0 million cap), preserving substantial non-dilutive cash flow during its critical commercialization ramp.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Overhead Calculation Methodologies
Salaries and Wages: Directly Engaged Personnel, Specified Employees, and the 10% Foreign Rule

Salaries and wages consistently represent the largest expenditure category in Canadian SR&ED claims. Pursuant to subsection 37(8) of the ITA and subsection 2900(2) of the ITR, a claimant may include the portion of salaries and wages paid to employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment, plus employer-paid statutory payroll contributions (such as Canada Pension Plan [CPP] contributions), but strictly excludes dividends, taxable benefits, retiring allowances, and self-employed contractor fees.
Allocation of Employee Time and the "All or Substantially All" (ASA) Rule

For arm's-length employees, salaries are prorated based on the percentage of their normal working hours spent directly on eligible SR&ED activities (including commensurate support work under paragraph 248(1)(d)). However, under subsection 2900(5) of the ITR, if an employee spends all or substantially all (ASA)—defined administratively by the CRA as 90% or more—of their employment time in the taxation year on the prosecution of SR&ED, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be included in the SR&ED expenditure pool and the Prescribed Proxy Amount salary base. Claimants must maintain contemporaneous time-tracking records—such as monthly timesheets, project codes, or sprint logs—to substantiate the claimed percentage for each employee, and for any founder claimed at all or substantially all of their time, the CRA expects specific evidentiary support for that individual.
Permissible Foreign SR&ED Salaries (10% Rule — Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA)

As a general rule, SR&ED must be prosecuted physically inside Canada. However, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA provides a narrow statutory exception for salaries and wages paid to Canadian-resident employees performing SR&ED work outside Canada (for example, an engineer employed by a Canadian corporation who travels to a foreign testing facility or field site to run experiments). Reported on Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661, total permissible foreign SR&ED salaries and wages are strictly capped at 10% of the total salaries and wages claimed for SR&ED performed in Canada (Lines 300 and 305) during the taxation year. Any foreign salary exceeding the 10% ceiling, or any payment to non-Canadian contractors outside Canada, is completely ineligible.
Specified Employees: Statutory Restrictions and 2026 YMPE Caps

To prevent owner-managers and controlling shareholders from artificially inflating SR&ED claims via year-end bonuses or excessive executive compensation, the ITA and ITR impose three stringent statutory restrictions on specified employees. Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" is an employee who is a specified shareholder of the employer—defined as a taxpayer who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time during the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of any corporation related to the corporation—or an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a family member who works in the business and does not deal at arm's length with the corporation, even if that family member owns zero shares). Importantly, share ownership at any single point in the taxation year triggers specified employee status; a founder diluted below the 10% threshold after a financing round may still be a specified employee for that year, requiring claimants to maintain a complete cap table showing the exact dates of every share issue or transfer.

First, under subsection 37(9) of the ITA (and CRA Guide T4088, Line 305), bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are strictly excluded from SR&ED expenditures. The CRA defines a bonus as an amount paid in addition to the employee's normal pay. Moreover, dividends paid to founder-shareholders do not constitute salary or wages under section 248(1) and earn zero SR&ED tax credits. Second, under subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages that can be claimed on Line 305 of Form T661 for a single specified employee cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the corporation's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee: maximum = A × B ÷ 365, where A is 5 times the YMPE and B is the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee.

For the 2026 calendar year, the CPP YMPE is $74,600.00 (with a CPP contribution rate of 5.95% outside Quebec), resulting in a maximum direct SR&ED salary cap of $373,000.00 (5 × $74,600.00) per specified employee for a full 365-day year.

Third, when a claimant elects the Proxy Method to calculate overhead, the amount of a specified employee's salary that may be included in the proxy salary base (Part 5 of Form T661) is further restricted under subsection 2900(7) of the ITR to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages from the corporation for the year (encompassing both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, but excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid salary or wages paid in the year under subsection 2900(9)) and 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual. Notably, under subsection 2900(7), proration is based on total days employed in the year, with no proration for the time during the year that the employee is not a specified employee: ceiling = 2.5 × A × B ÷ 365, where A is the YMPE and B is the number of days in the taxation year during which the individual was an employee of the claimant.

For a 2026 taxation year-end (2.5 × $74,600.00), the ceiling equals $186,500.00. Thus, if a specified employee founder earns a regular salary of $250,000 in 2026, 75% of their salary is $187,500, which is capped at $186,500 in Part 5 of Form T661. Furthermore, under subsections 2900(8) and 2900(10) of the ITR, if a specified employee of a corporation is also employed by an associated corporation (including deemed associated individuals related to the corporation or partnerships with related/associated partners) whose taxation year ends in the same calendar year, the 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500) proxy base ceiling cannot be exceeded in aggregate and must be shared between the associated employers.
Overhead Calculation Methodologies: The Proxy Method vs. The Traditional Method

Under section 37 of the ITA and section 2900 of the ITR, taxpayers must elect on Form T661 (Line 160 for the Proxy Method or Line 162 for the Traditional Method) how they will account for SR&ED overhead and other indirect expenditures.
The Proxy Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) to (VI) of the ITA; Subsection 2900(4) of the ITR)

Elected by the vast majority of Canadian SR&ED claimants, the Proxy Method eliminates the administrative burden of tracking, documenting, and defending individual overhead expenses. Instead, the claimant ticks Line 160 of Form T661, enters "0" on Line 360, and calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base. Historically, the PPA rate was 65% for 2012 and prior years, 60% for 2013, and has remained fixed at 55% since 2014 under subsection 2900(4) of the ITR.

Under the Proxy Method, the 55% PPA is not added to the section 37 deductible expenditure pool, because the actual underlying business overhead expenses—such as office utilities, clerical support, training costs, moving expenses, and retiring allowances—are already deducted directly in computing business income under subsection 9(1) of the ITA. Rather, the PPA is included directly in the definition of qualified expenditure under subsection 127(9) of the ITA (Part 4 of Form T661), where it earns the 35% or 15% federal SR&ED ITC. Under subsection 2900(6) of the ITR, the PPA is subject to an overall cap on the prescribed proxy amount.
The Traditional Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the ITA; Subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the ITR)

Taxpayers whose actual eligible SR&ED overhead exceeds 55% of their SR&ED salary base may elect the Traditional Method on Line 162 of Form T661. Under the Traditional Method, no PPA or salary base cap is calculated; instead, actual overhead and other expenditures are itemized and entered on Line 360 of Form T661, becoming part of both the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the section 127 qualified expenditure base for ITC purposes.

To qualify under the Traditional Method, an expenditure must either be all or substantially all (ASA) attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)), or be directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II)). Under paragraphs 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(b) of the ITR, an indirect expenditure is "directly attributable" to the prosecution of SR&ED (or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED) only if it satisfies two cumulative tests explained in the CRA's Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy and affirmed in Ergorecherche et Conseils Inc. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1710): first, the expenditure must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (arbitrary allocation methods are rejected); and second, the expenditure must be incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED, meaning it would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not occurred. Under the Traditional Method, claimants may include eligible employee training costs (section 6.5 of CRA policy), moving expenses to relocate SR&ED employees, taxable benefits related to selecting and hiring SR&ED personnel (section 6.4 of CRA policy), and retiring allowances, all of which are strictly barred from direct claim under the Proxy Method.

body.text: Materials Consumed or Transformed and Recapture Rules

Under both the Traditional Method (paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR) and the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA), a claimant may claim 100% of the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. As set out in the CRA's Materials Policy, to claim the cost of a material, the expenditure must be of a current nature (expenditures for the purchase of equipment, data, or a software licence are generally capital in nature rather than current materials). Materials may be purchased from either Canadian or foreign suppliers and claimed when used directly in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. If a property on which an SR&ED tax credit was calculated is subsequently disposed of or converted to commercial use, the taxpayer must report a recapture of the credit, which creates or increases tax otherwise payable (such as on Schedule 340 and Line 221 of Schedule 5 for Nova Scotia recapture, and corresponding federal recapture schedules).
Cloud Computing, SaaS Environments, and AI Training Costs

In modern software engineering, Software-as-a-Service (SaaS), and artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) claims, cloud computing expenditures—such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP)—represent a critical expenditure category. Under CRA guidance, cloud computing resources utilized directly for SR&ED activities (such as compute capacity, staging and test environments used for experimental work, and AI model training runs) qualify as eligible SR&ED expenditures (claimed as materials consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED).

However, CRA auditors require strict segregation between development/R&D cloud infrastructure and production cloud infrastructure. Production cloud infrastructure (AWS, GCP, or Azure hosting the live commercial product for customers) must be coded to Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) / Cost of Revenue, whereas only the development and staging environments used for experimental SR&ED work are eligible. Similarly, routine software subscriptions and using pre-built AI tools or APIs in a standard, routine manner—such as using ChatGPT to write emails or conducting business analytics—do not qualify for SR&ED. To substantiate cloud claims during a CRA review, claimants must export monthly AWS, GCP, or Azure cost reports with environment resource tags separating R&D/staging from production workloads. Furthermore, where startups utilize promotional cloud credits such as AWS Activate (which provides $1,000 USD to $5,000 USD for bootstrapped startups and up to $200,000 USD for VC- or accelerator-backed ventures), only actual net paid expenditures qualify for SR&ED ITCs.
Subcontractor and Third-Party Payments: The 80% Inclusion Rule and Geographic Restrictions

Payments made to an arm's-length Canadian contractor performing eligible SR&ED work on the claimant's behalf are 100% deductible in the section 37 pool (Part 3 of Form T661), but are claimable at 80% of the contract value (a 20% statutory reduction) when calculating qualified expenditures for the section 127 ITC (Part 4 of Form T661). Conversely, payments made to non-Canadian contractors performing work outside Canada are completely ineligible for SR&ED, and payments to non-arm's-length contractors are restricted from earning contract ITCs.
Restored Capital Expenditures (Post-December 16, 2024) and Accelerated CCA Classes

Under the rules in effect between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures were excluded from SR&ED eligibility. Under the reforms announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and enacted in Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026), capital expenditures have been restored on rules mirroring those that existed prior to 2014, applying to depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and in the case of rental/lease costs, amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024. To qualify, the property must be intended either to use all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in the performance of SR&ED in Canada. CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations eligible for the 35% SR&ED ITC within their expenditure limit are entitled to partial refundability of the credit at a rate of 40% on their eligible capital expenditures.

In addition to restoring SR&ED capital expenditures, Budget 2024 introduced an immediate 100% write-off for costs related to patents, data network infrastructure equipment, computers, and other data-processing equipment acquired on or after April 16, 2024, until January 1, 2027. For businesses acquiring technology and AI assets, three standard Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) classes are also directly relevant: Class 50 (55% declining balance rate for general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and AI hardware), Class 12 (100% deduction rate for application software and perpetual AI software licences, subject to the half-year rule where applicable), and Class 8 (20% declining balance rate for general peripheral equipment not fitting another class), whereas cloud-hosted SaaS subscriptions remain current operating expenses fully deductible in the year incurred.
The 180-Day Unpaid Amounts Rule (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26) of the ITA)

An SR&ED expenditure—including salaries, wages, and materials—can generate an investment tax credit in the taxation year only if the amount in respect of the expenditure is actually paid in the taxation year or within 180 days after the end of the taxation year. Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA and subsection 2900(9) of the ITR, unpaid remuneration accrued at year-end that is not paid within 180 days is excluded from both qualified expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount salary base.
Judicial Precedents, Case Law Evolution, and CRA Audit Defence
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998) and the Five-Question Test

While subsection 248(1) of the ITA supplies the statutory text, the operational legal test applied by CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) and Canadian courts to evaluate SR&ED eligibility was established by Judge Donald Bowman (as he then was) of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, [1998] T.C.J. No. 340 (QL). Judge Bowman articulated five cumulative criteria—universally known as the "Five-Question Test"—to determine whether a particular activity constitutes SR&ED.

First, was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? At paragraph 39 of subsequent decisions citing paragraph 16 of Northwest Hydraulic, courts emphasize that if the resolution of a technical problem is achievable through standard procedures or routine engineering known to competent professionals in the field, no technological uncertainty exists. Second, did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? Third, did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? Fourth, did the process result in a technological advancement? Crucially, a project satisfies this fourth criterion if it results in a scientific or technological advancement even if the experiment failed commercially or technically—in fact, the dividing line between routine engineering and SR&ED is often whether the experiment could have failed. Fifth, was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?
Appellate Codification and Doctrinal Refinements in the Tax Court of Canada

Following Northwest Hydraulic, appellate and trial rulings have refined how the Five-Question Test applies across diverse industries. In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2000 DTC 2372 (TCC), aff'd by the Federal Court of Appeal), the Federal Court of Appeal formally summarized and endorsed Judge Bowman's five criteria from Northwest Hydraulic as the governing national standard, holding that work stemming entirely from standard practice cannot yield the technological advancement required by the SR&ED definition. In Ergorecherche et Conseils Inc. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1710), the Tax Court established the strict "direct linkage" and "incremental" requirements for claiming overhead under the Traditional Method pursuant to paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the ITR, rejecting arbitrary overhead allocation formulas.

Subsequent Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence has clarified the legal status of contemporaneous documentation under the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion. In Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313), which involved shop-floor conditioning and packaging equipment modifications, Justice Jorré held at paragraph 94 that although contemporaneous documentation may be necessary to resolve factual disputes between the parties, "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific intent, is not a condition to the recognition of scientific research or experimental development".

In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6), Justice Sommerfeldt provided an exhaustive doctrinal synthesis of the first, second, third, and fifth criteria. At paragraph 17, Justice Sommerfeldt noted the absence of a statutory definition of "routine engineering"; at paragraph 26, after reviewing the jurisprudence, he concluded that a "hypothesis" is simply "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial"; at paragraph 33, he summarized the characteristics required to demonstrate that the scientific method was adopted; and at paragraph 46, he reaffirmed that while contemporaneous documentation of the claimed work is important as the best evidence, a written contemporaneous record may not be absolutely essential in every case.

More recently, in Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC, Docket 2018-677), the Tax Court applied Judge Bowman's five criteria in favour of a frozen pie manufacturer conducting formulation and thermal processing experiments, demonstrating that shop-floor food manufacturing trials qualify for SR&ED when systematic investigation is required to overcome technical uncertainties. Finally, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 159, Docket 2023-2126(IT)I; amended reasons January 17, 2025), involving experimentation to control microbial growth and achieve a room-temperature shelf-stable vinegar-based drink, the Minister had denied the claim on the basis that the preservatives were known to competent professionals and that records were inadequate. Ruling for the appellant, Justice Bodie held that the taxpayer satisfied all five questions and established a vital evidentiary clarification: contemporaneous documentation is meant to keep track of the hypotheses generated, experiments undertaken to test those hypotheses, and results obtained as work progresses—it does not need to be designed for someone unfamiliar with a specific field of science or technology to replicate the results.

body.text: Governing Bodies, Administrative Filing Procedures, and Audit Mechanics
Institutional Division of Labour and CRA Review Architecture

In Canada, the administration of R&D tax incentives involves a clear institutional division of labour between the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates tax policy and drafts legislation, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers the federal SR&ED program as well as harmonized provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (such as those in Ontario, British Columbia, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and the Yukon). Within the CRA, technical eligibility reviews are conducted by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) operating under the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, while expenditure and tax calculations are audited by Financial Reviewers.

To assist businesses in navigating compliance and mitigating audit risk, the CRA offers two specialized advisory services. The First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) provides dedicated educational guidance to first-time SR&ED claimants on eligibility criteria and documentation standards, while the Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC) service—which replaced the legacy Pre-Claim Project Review (PCPR)—enables claimants to request an upfront consultation with the CRA after completing a self-assessment to determine whether their R&D work is eligible prior to submitting a formal claim.
Prescribed Tax Forms and the Structure of Form T661

Corporations claiming SR&ED must submit their claim with their T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (electronically via the CRA's Corporation Internet Filing service) using Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), Schedule 31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations), and Schedule 5 (Tax Calculation Supplementary – Corporations), alongside any applicable provincial or territorial credit schedules.
As specified in the CRA's Filing Requirements Policy and Guide T4088, Form T661 comprises ten parts (with Parts 1 through 8 detailed below):

body.text: The Strict 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline and Processing Timelines

Under the Income Tax Act, a claimant has a strict statutory reporting deadline of 18 months after the end of the fiscal year in which the SR&ED expenditures were incurred to file Form T661 and Schedule 31 (as well as harmonized provincial schedules such as Ontario Schedule 566, Nova Scotia Schedule 340, and Yukon Schedule 442). Beyond this 18-month window, the SR&ED claim is permanently statute-barred—there are no extensions.

Once filed, refundable CCPC claims that are processed without a detailed technical review typically take 120 to 270 days from the fiscal year-end to issue a refund, whereas claims selected for a technical review by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor generally require 12 to 18 months from the date of filing.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes
In addition to the federal SR&ED ITC, Canadian provinces and the Yukon Territory offer supplementary R&D tax credits that piggyback on or parallel the federal regime.
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario provides three corporate R&D tax credits enacted under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and administered by the CRA. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC)—governed by section 96 (specifically subsections 96(3.1), 96(8), 96(12), and 96(14)) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and claimed on Schedule 566 (entered on Line 468 of Schedule 5)—provides an 8% refundable tax credit (for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016; reduced from 10% for taxation years ending before June 1, 2016) on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, yielding a maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000. Associated corporations must share the $3 million expenditure limit, and the limit is gradually phased out if prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or if prior-year taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Crucially, Ontario updated the OITC qualified expenditure definition to harmonize with the federal capital restoration: OITC qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures, 40% of qualified capital expenditures made before January 1, 2014, exclude capital expenditures made between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, and include 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024. A corporation may also waive the current-year OITC in whole or in part under subsection 96(14).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC)—claimed on Schedule 508—is a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures, with unused credits eligible for a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC)—claimed on Schedule 568 together with a separate Schedule 569 (Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit Contract Information) for each eligible contract—provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under eligible R&D contracts with approved Ontario research institutes.
Quebec: Independent Administration by Revenu Québec

Quebec administers its R&D tax incentives independently through Revenu Québec. For taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025, under Form RD-1029.7-V (Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D)), Quebec provided a 100% refundable tax credit at a base rate of 14%, rising up to an enhanced rate of 30% on eligible R&D salaries and wages (and 50% of arm's-length Quebec subcontractor payments) incurred in Quebec, subject to a sizable exclusion threshold. For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, that credit has been replaced by the refundable tax credit for research, innovation and commercialization (CRIC), claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR, at 30% on qualified expenditures above the exclusion threshold up to $1 million and 20% on qualified expenditures above that amount. Notably, in the review of tax expenditures accompanying its 2025–2026 budget, aimed at achieving $2.9 billion in savings over five years, the Quebec provincial government consolidated eight existing tax measures, including its R&D tax credits, into the CRIC rather than eliminating its R&D support.
British Columbia, Alberta, the Prairie Provinces, Atlantic Canada, and the Yukon

Across Western, Atlantic, and Northern Canada, corporations can access substantial provincial and territorial R&D tax credits administered primarily by the CRA. In British Columbia, corporations claim the BC SR&ED Tax Credit on Schedule 425 (Form T666), which provides a 10% refundable credit for qualifying CCPCs and a 10% non-refundable credit for other corporations (with the portion of the BCRDTC arising from the federal Prescribed Proxy Amount tracked on Part 5, Line 13 of Form T666/Schedule 425, and capital BC qualified expenditures reported on Line 360). Importantly, the legislative eligibility period for the BC SR&ED credit, which was scheduled to expire on September 1, 2022, was extended to September 1, 2027.

In Atlantic Canada, Nova Scotia provides a 15% fully refundable Research and Development Tax Credit available to all corporations regardless of size on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Nova Scotia, claimed on Schedule 340 within 18 months of the tax year-end and entered on Line 566 of Schedule 5 (with any property recapture calculated on Schedule 340 and reported on Line 221 of Schedule 5). Similarly, New Brunswick provides a 15% fully refundable Research and Development Tax Credit claimed on Schedule 360, and Newfoundland and Labrador provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit claimed on Schedule 301 (Form T1129). In Manitoba, corporations claim the Manitoba R&D tax credit on Schedule 380. Finally, in the Yukon Territory, corporations claim the Yukon Research and Development Tax Credit on Schedule 442 within 18 months of year-end (entered on Line 698 of Schedule 5), which provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in the Yukon plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on eligible expenditures paid or payable to Yukon University.

body.text: Interaction with Direct Grants, Assistance Stacking, and Comprehensive Financial Modelling
Stacking Mechanics: NRC IRAP and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Optimization

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, government assistance (including provincial R&D tax credits and federal or provincial direct grants) and non-government assistance must be deducted when computing qualified SR&ED expenditures. Canada's premier direct R&D grant program for small- and medium-sized enterprises is the National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which covers up to 80% of eligible internal R&D salaries and up to 50% of eligible subcontractor costs (and received an additional $100 million in Budget 2024 for the NRC IRAP AI Assist Program).

When stacking NRC IRAP contributions with SR&ED under the Proxy Method, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 is computed on the eligible SR&ED salary base prior to deducting the NRC IRAP grant in Part 4. Consequently, even when NRC IRAP reimburses 80% of an employee's direct SR&ED salary, the claimant still generates the full 55% PPA overhead credit base on 100% of that employee's SR&ED salary, leaving 75% of the salary value (100% + 55% − 80%) inside the net qualified expenditure pool to earn federal and provincial SR&ED tax credits.
Comprehensive 2026 End-to-End Financial Calculation Case Study (Ontario Qualifying CCPC)

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics of a fully integrated 2026 federal and provincial SR&ED claim under the modernized Bill C-15 regime (for a taxation year ending December 31, 2026, where the 2026 CPP YMPE is $74,600.00), consider an Ontario-based CCPC with prior-year taxable income below $500,000 and prior-year taxable capital below $15,000,000 (qualifying for 100% of the $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit and 100% of the $3,000,000 Ontario OITC expenditure limit) that elects the Proxy Method on Line 160 of Form T661. During 2026, the corporation incurs $400,000 in arm's-length SR&ED developer salaries (Line 300), pays its founder/specified employee a $250,000 base salary for 100% dedicated SR&ED work (Line 305: direct salary is $250,000, below the ceiling; Part 5 proxy base is the lesser of $187,500 (75% × $250,000) and $186,500 (2.5 × $74,600), fixing the founder's proxy base at $186,500), incurs $18,000 in tagged R&D cloud computing environments (AWS/GCP/Azure) as materials consumed (Line 320), pays $60,000 to an arm's-length Canadian contractor for SR&ED work ($60,000 on Line 340 in Part 3; $48,000 in Part 4), and acquires $100,000 in eligible SR&ED capital equipment after December 16, 2024 (100% eligible for OITC and federal SR&ED, with the 35% federal ITC on capital being 40% refundable).

body.text: Strategic Conclusions and Audit Compliance Framework

Canada's federal and provincial R&D tax architecture underscores a critical operational imperative for corporate executives, tax directors, and legal counsel: while the legislative reforms enacted through Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) have substantially expanded the financial ceiling of the SR&ED program—elevating the enhanced 35% expenditure limit up to $6 million, broadening the taxable capital phase-out band to $15 million–$75 million, extending 35% refundability to eligible Canadian public corporations, and restoring capital expenditures—the CRA's technical and financial audit enforcement remains uncompromisingly rigorous.

To maximize claim recovery and insulate filings against adverse adjustments during a joint CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer audit, Canadian claimants must institutionalize five core compliance protocols across their engineering and accounting workflows. First, technical narratives in Part 2 of Form T661 must be framed strictly around technological uncertainty rather than commercial value or marketing features, demonstrating why the system-level constraint could not be resolved by routine engineering or standard practice under Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies. Second, claimants must capture contemporaneous documentation in real time—such as architecture decision records, experiment logs, version control histories, and sprint notes—in accordance with the evidentiary principles established in Joel Theatrical Rigging and Manning Canning Kitchens.

Third, founder-led corporations must structure specified employee compensation proactively through regular T4 payroll rather than dividends or year-end bonuses (which are statutorily barred under subsection 37(9)), calibrating base salaries to the 2026 YMPE caps of $373,000 for direct SR&ED salary (subsection 37(9.1)) and $186,500 for the proxy salary base (ITR subsection 2900(7)), and ensuring all accrued wages are paid within 180 days of year-end. Fourth, software and AI startups claiming cloud computing costs (AWS, GCP, Azure) must enforce automated environment-level resource tagging to segregate eligible R&D/staging instances from commercial production COGS, while ensuring all subcontractor work is performed inside Canada by arm's-length Canadian entities. Finally, corporate tax calendars must strictly respect the non-negotiable 18-month statutory filing deadline from fiscal year-end for Form T661, Schedule 31, and provincial schedules, ensuring zero forfeiture of statutory R&D entitlements.
